Super Micro Computer has swung from a very large 5 year gain to a sharp pullback over the past year. This puts the spotlight squarely on whether the current share price is still in line with what its earnings can support. With legal scrutiny around export controls now intersecting with its role in high end AI hardware, the key issue for you as an investor is how much of the past story the market can still reasonably expect the business to earn through its income statement.

Over 5 years the stock has returned about 446.4%. The valuation question now is how much of that move can be backed up by the level and quality of earnings the business is producing today.

Ongoing Department of Justice investigations into alleged Nvidia chip smuggling may influence future profitability through potential legal costs, management focus, and any change in access to restricted AI components that feed into Super Micro Computer's earnings power.

Your read on Super Micro Computer is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Super Micro Computer's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether the current price for Super Micro Computer is justified by its earnings when judged against the Fair Ratio benchmark.

If you want more context around Super Micro Computer and the AI hardware theme, a focused stock screen of 53 AI infrastructure stocks may be helpful.

Does Super Micro Computer Look Undervalued on Earnings?

The P/E multiple is a straightforward way to compare what you pay for each dollar of Super Micro Computer earnings with peers in Tech. On this yardstick, the stock trades at about 4.5x earnings, far below both the wider Tech sector on roughly 14.9x and the peer average near 37.0x. This implies the market is attaching a much lower price tag to its profit stream than to comparable businesses.

The Fair Ratio model, which adjusts for Super Micro Computer's growth profile, profitability, size and risk, points to a materially higher P/E than where the shares change hands today, so the stock screens as undervalued on this framework. Because the current Department of Justice investigation into alleged Nvidia chip smuggling has pressured sentiment and raised perceived risk, that gap suggests investors are heavily discounting future earnings relative to what the fundamentals alone would indicate. However, rather than chasing stocks that have already rebounded sharply, investors may also want to look beyond the technology rally for fundamentally strong companies trading at attractive valuations. This creates an opportunity to identify undervalued stocks with improving earnings outlooks before the broader market fully recognizes their potential.

In periods of heightened market volatility and economic uncertainty, value investing can offer an attractive alternative to growth- or momentum-driven strategies. When investors sell stocks amid broader market concerns, fundamentally sound companies can become available at discounted valuations, creating opportunities for value investors to capitalize on their long-term earnings potential.

However, identifying genuinely undervalued stocks requires more than simply looking for low share prices or valuation multiples. Several stocks that have delivered significant gains in the past demonstrate the potential of this investment strategy. Here, we discuss four stocks — Arrow Electronics, Super Micro Computer, BP plc and Ingram Micro Holding Corp. — that have qualified our PEG-driven screening criteria.

However, this apparently simple value investment technique has some drawbacks and not understanding the strategy properly may often lead to "value traps." In such a situation, these value picks start to underperform over the long run as the temporary problems, which once drove the share price down, turn out to be persistent.

Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) stock is down 48% from its early October peak, even though the company beat estimates with $115.8 billion of quarterly revenue.

Scott Galloway predicted on Pivot that the stock will be up at the end of the year.

Analysts are still raising EPS estimates, the stock trades at 9x forward earnings, and Super Micro Computer's (SMCI:NASDAQ) sales point to strong demand.

The California probe and China scrutiny that also reaches AMD (AMD:NASDAQ) are the risks, but a year-end close above today's price looks likely.

Nvidia just had the biggest quarter in its history, and its stock can't stop falling.

Founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and the board reinstated him on Nov. 23. The selloff had pulled down rival AMD and server maker Super Micro Computer too.

Pivot co-host Scott Galloway, who argued this week that Nvidia has the widest moat in AI, thinks the sellers will lose this one. He pointed to Apple, which Tim Cook grew 15x after Steve Jobs died, then made his call:

"My prediction actually is that NVIDIA does better and that the stock's up at the end of the year."

We'll be able to check that in about six weeks.

Investing.com — November has been brutal for AI hardware. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares have tumbled 40.8% over the past month, and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 as U.S. Justice Department probes tied to AI chip sales to China widened. The hardest legal questions, however, sit with Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), the AI server assembler whose senior executives were criminally indicted in March over alleged chip diversion to China. Its shares fell another 19.4% this week to $21.65, and the 30-day loss now stands at 35.8%.

Super Micro's 4.3x trailing P/E looks like a typographical error, but the market is pricing a legal overhang and a cash-hungry business model that the headline growth forecasts leave out. Analysts forecast 97.2% revenue growth and 130.0% EPS growth. Beneath InvestingPro's $36.71 intrinsic valuation, though, sits a balance sheet with 33.2% total debt-to-capital and razor-thin server assembly margins that compress whenever component costs rise.

Those margins are where InvestingPro's AI stock picker, ProPicks AI, looks before it looks at any P/E, and on that measure Super Micro missed the cut for November's Tech Titans, a list reserved for high-margin tech leaders, ahead of the stock's 36% wipeout. The places went to chip-equipment and IT services companies that keep far more of every sale.

See which chip-equipment and IT services stocks the AI picker chose over Super Micro for November: Explore the Tech Titans strategy on InvestingPro

Fast to Market, Thin on Margin

Super Micro makes its money building complete AI server racks around the newest chips faster than its rivals, and that speed is its moat.

First-quarter fiscal 2027 results proved that speed is pulling in demand at scale. Revenue jumped to $19.9 billion, up 298% year-over-year and 79% sequentially, far above guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion, although roughly $2.3 billion reflected catch-up from previously deferred deployments. Non-GAAP EPS of $1.81 topped the $1.23 forecast by 47%, AI solutions climbed to 71% of revenue from 59% the prior quarter, and management raised full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $72 billion to $82 billion from $65 billion to $72 billion.

Wall Street's Rebound Case Meets a Lower Fair Value

Wall Street mostly treats the sell-off as overdone. Raymond James rates Super Micro a Buy at $65, Rosenblatt at $57, and Needham at $46, while Mizuho holds at $36 and Susquehanna rates it a Sell at $18. The median price target of $43.60 sits well above the share price.

Key Takeaways

Super Micro stock is down 23% in 2026, even after a record $19.9 billion quarter and a fiscal 2027 revenue outlook raised to $72-82 billion.

An export case against people tied to the company, a $5.6 billion stock and preferred raise, lower margins and Nvidia's leadership crisis erased a gain that stood at 41% in early October.

Dell's AI server revenue alone was bigger than Super Micro's whole quarter, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise's margin warning suggests thin AI server margins are a problem for the whole group.

At under 4x forward earnings, the stock looks due for a bounce if the fiscal second quarter lands inside guidance, but the legal overhang argues for a small position.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) just reported the biggest quarter in its history, and its stock is still down 23% in 2026.

In early October, TIKR had it up 41% for the year. And AI servers haven't stopped selling: Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE:NYSE) both just raised their outlooks, and Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ), whose chips fill Super Micro's racks, guided to about $130 billion of January-quarter revenue. Investors doubt Super Micro can keep the profits.

A year of self-inflicted wounds

In March, the Justice Department charged three people tied to Super Micro, including a co-founder, with diverting about $2.5 billion of U.S. AI technology to China. The company isn't charged, and a board-led probe found no evidence that current senior management knew. Then in June, Super Micro launched a $5.6 billion raise of stock and mandatory convertible preferred. The business won back much of that ground, with more than $60 billion of new orders in the June quarter and an Oct. 20 preannouncement well above what analysts expected.
